# About this tutorial

A **hit** is a gene whose barcodes change consistently in the treated samples
compared with the control samples. In a dropout (loss of function) screen the
interesting hits are usually depleted: their knockdown kills the cells only in
the presence of the treatment.

This tutorial explains, step by step:

1. how to tell ScreenR which samples to compare;
2. the statistical methods to find hits and how to read their results;
3. how to combine the methods;
4. how to check the candidate hits before trusting them.

It continues from the object of the previous tutorials:

```{r object, message=FALSE}
library(ScreenR)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)

data(count_table)
data(annotation_table)

counts <- count_table
colnames(counts) <- c(
    "Barcode", "Time1", "Time2", "Time3_TRT_A", "Time3_TRT_B", "Time3_TRT_C",
    "Time3_CTRL_A", "Time3_CTRL_B", "Time3_CTRL_C",
    "Time4_TRT_A", "Time4_TRT_B", "Time4_TRT_C",
    "Time4_CTRL_A", "Time4_CTRL_B", "Time4_CTRL_C"
)
counts <- filter(counts, Barcode != "*")
groups <- factor(c(
    "T1/T2", "T1/T2",
    rep("Time3_TRT", 3), rep("Time3_CTRL", 3),
    rep("Time4_TRT", 3), rep("Time4_CTRL", 3)
))

object <- create_screenr_object(
    table = counts, annotation = annotation_table, groups = groups
)
object <- remove_all_zero_row(object)
object <- normalize_data(object)
object <- compute_data_table(object)
```

# Overview of the methods

| Method | Function | Unit | Gives an FDR | Uses replicates |
|--------|----------|------|--------------|-----------------|
| Gene-level Z-score test | `find_gene_zscore_hit()` | Compares the mean Z-score of the barcodes of each gene with random sets of barcodes | Yes | With `compute_barcode_statistics()` |
| CAMERA | `find_camera_hit()` | Tests whether the barcodes of a gene change more than the others | Yes | Yes |
| ROAST | `find_roast_hit()` | Tests whether the barcodes of a gene change | Yes | Yes |
| Time course | `find_time_hit()` | Tests whether the treatment effect changes over time | Yes | Yes |
| Legacy Z-score rules | `find_zscore_hit()`, `find_robust_zscore_hit()` | Counts barcodes below the median Z-score | No | No |

The **FDR** (false discovery rate) is the expected proportion of false hits
among the genes you call hits: with an FDR cut off of 5%, about 1 in 20 of the
reported genes is expected to be a false positive. Each method returns only the
genes with `FDR <= fdr` (default 0.05); use `fdr = 1` to get all the genes and
rank them yourself.

# Step 1: which samples to compare

CAMERA, ROAST and the replicate-aware statistics use a linear model, which
needs two things:

* a **design matrix**, which says which group each sample belongs to;
* a **contrast**, which says which groups to compare.

`create_design_matrix()` builds the design matrix from the groups of the
object: one column per group, and a 1 in the column of the group of each
sample. Group names that are not valid R names are changed (`T1/T2` becomes
`T1.T2`).

```{r design}
design <- create_design_matrix(object)
design
```

`create_contrast()` builds the comparison between groups by name: here
treated against control at each time point.

```{r contrasts}
contrast_time3 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time3_TRT", control = "Time3_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4 <- create_contrast(design,
    treatment = "Time4_TRT", control = "Time4_CTRL"
)
contrast_time4
```

The contrast gives +1 to the treated group and -1 to the control group: the
result is the treated minus the control. With several groups on one side
(for example `treatment = c("Time3_TRT", "Time4_TRT")`) their average is used.

**Common mistake.** Do not build the design with `model.matrix(~ groups)` and
rename its columns: the first group becomes the intercept and the columns are
in alphabetical order, so the names end up on the wrong columns and the wrong
samples are compared. `create_design_matrix()` and `create_contrast()` avoid
this.

The examples below compare treated and control samples at Time4.

# Step 2: the Z-score method

## Fold changes and Z-scores

`compute_metrics()` averages the replicates of the treated and of the control
samples of one time point and computes for each barcode:

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `Treated`, `Control` | Mean normalized count |
| `Log2FC` | log2((Treated + 0.5) / (Control + 0.5)): negative means depleted in the treated samples |
| `Zscore` | Log2FC standardized with the mean and standard deviation of all barcodes |
| `ZscoreRobust` | Log2FC standardized with the median and MAD, less sensitive to outliers |

The `treatment` and `control` arguments are values of the Treatment column of
`get_sample_table()`, and `day` a value of its Day column.

```{r metrics}
metrics_time4 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time4"
)
head(metrics_time4)
```

`plot_zscore_distribution()` compares the Z-scores of several time points: a
treatment with an effect gives a longer left tail at the later time point.

```{r zscore-distribution}
metrics_time3 <- compute_metrics(object,
    control = "CTRL", treatment = "TRT", day = "Time3"
)
plot_zscore_distribution(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    alpha = 0.6
)
```

## Gene-level test

`find_gene_zscore_hit()` computes for each gene the mean Z-score of its
barcodes and asks how often a random set of barcodes of the same size has a
score at least as low (`direction = "Down"`). The random sets are drawn many
times (`n_permutations`), so the p-value needs no assumption on the
distribution of the Z-scores; `seed` makes it reproducible. The p-values are
then corrected for testing many genes (FDR).

If the library has control genes, their gene name can be given with
`control_genes` (for example `control_genes = "non-targeting"`): the random
sets are then drawn from the controls, which cannot contain true hits. Do this
only if the controls behave like genes without effect. Non-targeting shRNAs
often do not: targeting shRNAs are usually somewhat depleted compared with
them, so every gene looks depleted (in the K562 screen of ScreenR this called
hundreds of non-essential genes). Check first that the controls have the same
scores as genes known to have no effect; when in doubt, keep the default. `statistic = "median"` uses the median instead
of the mean, which is less affected by a single barcode with a strong
(possibly off-target) effect.

With `reference = "empirical"` the gene scores are compared with an
empirical null instead: the distribution of the scores of the genes without
effect, estimated from the centre of the distribution of all the genes
(`plot_empirical_null()` shows it). The hits do not make it conservative, and
it accounts for the barcodes of a gene varying together, which makes the
random sets of barcodes give too small p-values, especially in shRNA screens
(see `?find_gene_zscore_hit` and [Tutorial 4](Tutorial_4_CRISPR_screens.html)).
It needs a library with hundreds of genes, most of them without effect.

```{r gene-zscore}
gene_zscore <- find_gene_zscore_hit(metrics_time4, fdr = 1, seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore)
```

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `NBarcodes` | Number of barcodes of the gene |
| `Score` | Mean Z-score of the barcodes |
| `Log2FC` | Median log2 fold change of the barcodes |
| `PValue`, `FDR` | Significance |

## Using the replicates

`compute_metrics()` averages the replicates, so it cannot tell a consistent
barcode from a noisy one. `compute_barcode_statistics()` tests each barcode
with edgeR, using the variability between replicates, and returns a Z-score
that can be used by `find_gene_zscore_hit()` in the same way. This is the
recommended input.

```{r barcode-statistics}
barcode_statistics <- compute_barcode_statistics(
    object, design, contrast_time4
)
head(barcode_statistics)

gene_zscore_edger <- find_gene_zscore_hit(barcode_statistics, fdr = 1,
    seed = 1)
head(gene_zscore_edger)
```

## Legacy rules

`find_zscore_hit()` and `find_robust_zscore_hit()` call a gene a hit when more
than `number_barcode` of its barcodes are below the median Z-score. They are
kept for compatibility, but they do not give a p-value and many genes without
an effect pass them by chance (about 17% with 10 barcodes and
`number_barcode = 6`): prefer `find_gene_zscore_hit()`.

```{r legacy}
nrow(find_zscore_hit(metrics_time4, number_barcode = 6))
```

# Step 3: CAMERA and ROAST

Both test the barcodes of each gene as a set, using edgeR on the raw counts.

* **CAMERA** asks whether the barcodes of a gene change **more than the other
  barcodes** (a competitive test), taking into account the correlation between
  barcodes.
* **ROAST** asks whether the barcodes of a gene **change at all** (a
  self-contained test). It uses random rotations: set `seed` to get the same
  result every time, and use many rotations (`nrot`, default 9999) for a real
  analysis; here 999 keep the tutorial fast. With `method = "fry"` the same
  test is computed exactly, without rotations: it is faster and its p-values
  are not limited by the number of rotations.

CAMERA becomes conservative when many genes have an effect, because the other
barcodes it compares with then include true hits; ROAST and fry do not have
this limitation. On the other hand ROAST and fry test each gene on its own
barcodes, so they rely on the variability between replicates: they need
replicates in both groups, have little power with two replicates or noisy
data, and find almost nothing when the control is a single sample (for
example a plasmid library). The p-values of all three are one-sided, for the requested
direction.

`number_barcode` sets the minimum number of barcodes (more than
`number_barcode`) a gene needs to be tested, and `direction` chooses depleted
(`"Down"`) or enriched (`"Up"`) genes.

```{r camera-roast}
camera <- find_camera_hit(object, design, contrast_time4, fdr = 1)
head(camera)

roast <- find_roast_hit(object, design, contrast_time4,
    nrot = 999, seed = 42, fdr = 1
)
head(select(roast, Gene, NGenes, PropDown, PropUp, Direction, PValue, FDR,
    Log2FC))
```

| Column | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| `NGenes` | Number of barcodes of the gene |
| `Direction` | Down or Up |
| `PValue`, `FDR` | Significance |
| `PropDown`, `PropUp` (ROAST) | Proportion of barcodes going down or up |
| `Log2FC` | Median log2 fold change of the barcodes |

How many genes pass different FDR cut offs:

```{r fdr-levels}
fdr_levels <- c(0.05, 0.1, 0.25)
tibble(
    FDR = fdr_levels,
    zscore = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(gene_zscore_edger$FDR <= x),
        1L),
    CAMERA = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(camera$FDR <= x), 1L),
    ROAST = vapply(fdr_levels, function(x) sum(roast$FDR <= x), 1L)
)
```

The effect of the treatment in this example is weak: no gene reaches an FDR of
5%. In the rest of the tutorial we use 25% to illustrate the steps; in your
own analysis, choose the cut off before looking at the results and report it.

```{r alpha}
alpha <- 0.25
```

# Step 4: the time course

When the screen has several time points, `find_time_hit()` asks whether the
treatment effect **changes over time**, with one model for all the time points
instead of one analysis per time point. Untreated and treated samples each
follow a line over time; the method tests the difference between the slopes.
Early samples taken before the treatment can be added as `baseline`. The time
points are given in order with `days` and are treated as equally spaced.

```{r time}
time_hit <- find_time_hit(object,
    treatment = "TRT", control = "CTRL",
    baseline = c("Time1", "Time2"),
    days = c("Time1", "Time2", "Time3", "Time4"),
    fdr = 1
)
head(time_hit)
```

Here `Log2FC` is the change of the treatment log2 fold change per time point:
a negative value means that the depletion grows over time. In this dataset
`r sum(time_hit$FDR <= 0.05)` genes have an FDR below 5%
(`r paste(time_hit$Gene[time_hit$FDR <= 0.05], collapse = ", ")`): the time
course model is more powerful here than the comparison at a single time
point, because it uses all the samples.

# Step 5: combining the methods

The methods look at the data in different ways, so genes found by several of
them are the most convincing. `plot_common_hit()` shows the overlap between
the hits of three methods:

```{r venn, fig.height = 5}
plot_common_hit(
    hit_zscore = filter(gene_zscore_edger, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_camera = filter(camera, FDR <= alpha),
    hit_roast = filter(roast, FDR <= alpha),
    show_elements = FALSE, show_percentage = FALSE
)
```

`find_common_hit()` returns the genes found by at least `common_in` methods:

```{r common}
common <- find_common_hit(
    filter(gene_zscore_edger, FDR <= alpha),
    filter(camera, FDR <= alpha),
    filter(roast, FDR <= alpha),
    common_in = 2
)
common
```

`summarise_hits()` puts the FDR of every method in one table. `NMethods` counts
the methods in which the gene passes the cut off, and `MaxFDR` (the largest
FDR) is a conservative score to rank the genes supported by all the methods.
Pass the tables computed with `fdr = 1`, so that every gene has a value.

```{r summary}
summary <- summarise_hits(
    list(
        zscore = gene_zscore_edger, camera = camera,
        roast = roast, time = time_hit
    ),
    fdr = alpha
)
head(summary, 10)
```

The column `Hit` is `TRUE` when the gene passes the cut off in every method
(`MaxFDR <= alpha`). A note on interpretation: the combined list does not have
a guaranteed false discovery rate, so treat it as a short list of candidates
to validate. In this dataset `r sum(summary$Hit)` gene(s) pass all four
methods at 25%, so below we check the genes found by at least two of the
three methods of the Venn diagram.

# Step 6: checking the candidates

Statistics can produce false positives, so look at the data of each candidate.

```{r candidates}
candidates <- head(common, 2)
candidates
```

## Trend over time

`plot_trend()` shows the mean frequency of the barcodes of a gene in the chosen
samples (`group_var` takes values of the Treatment column). A depleted hit goes
down in the treated samples but not in the controls.

```{r trend, fig.height = 4}
plot_trend(object,
    genes = candidates, group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "TRT"),
    nrow = 1, ncol = 2
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    ggtitle("Treated samples")

plot_trend(object,
    genes = candidates, group_var = c("Time1", "Time2", "CTRL"),
    nrow = 1, ncol = 2
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1)) +
    ggtitle("Control samples")
```

## Distribution of the barcodes

`plot_boxplot()` shows the frequencies of all the barcodes of a gene in each
sample:

```{r boxplot, fig.height = 4}
plot_boxplot(object,
    genes = candidates[1], group_var = c("TRT", "CTRL"),
    fill_var = "Treatment"
) +
    theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1))
```

## Barcode by barcode

A real hit should be supported by most of its barcodes, not by one or two.
`plot_barcode_trend()` shows the log2 fold change of each barcode over the
time points:

```{r barcode-trend, fig.height = 4}
plot_barcode_trend(
    list(Time3 = metrics_time3, Time4 = metrics_time4),
    genes = candidates[1]
)
```

`plot_barcode_hit()` ranks all the barcodes by their log2 fold change and
places the barcodes of a gene on the ranking (vertical lines): most lines on
the left side means that the gene is depleted. The line on top shows where
the barcodes of the gene are concentrated (above 1, dashed line), and the
bottom panel shows their log2 fold changes (`show_log2fc = FALSE` hides it):

```{r barcode-hit, fig.height = 5}
plot_barcode_hit(object, design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, gene = candidates[1]
)
```

`find_discordant_barcodes()` lists the barcodes that behave very differently
from the other barcodes of their gene, which may have off-target effects:

```{r discordant}
discordant <- find_discordant_barcodes(metrics_time4, threshold = 3)
filter(discordant, Gene %in% candidates)
```

## Additional filters

Two filters can remove candidates that are not convincing:

* `filter_by_slope()` keeps the genes whose frequency decreases more over time
  in the treated samples than in the control samples;
* `filter_by_variance()` removes the genes whose barcodes disagree too much
  (variance of the barcode log2 fold changes above `variance`).

```{r filters}
filter_by_slope(object,
    genes = candidates,
    group_var_treatment = c("Time1", "Time2", "TRT"),
    group_var_control = c("Time1", "Time2", "CTRL")
)

filter_by_variance(object,
    genes = candidates, matrix_model = design,
    contrast = contrast_time4, variance = 0.5
) %>%
    distinct(Gene, Variance)
```

# Summary

| Step | What to do |
|------|------------|
| 1 | `create_design_matrix()` and `create_contrast()` for the comparison |
| 2 | `compute_barcode_statistics()` + `find_gene_zscore_hit()` |
| 3 | `find_camera_hit()` and `find_roast_hit()` (with `seed`) |
| 4 | `find_time_hit()` if there are several time points |
| 5 | `plot_common_hit()` and `summarise_hits()` |
| 6 | `plot_trend()`, `plot_boxplot()`, `plot_barcode_trend()`, `plot_barcode_hit()`, `find_discordant_barcodes()` |

Choose the FDR cut off before the analysis, report it, and validate the
candidates experimentally.

```{r session}
sessionInfo()
```
